opus-5.5.text:
I think the role of human mathematicians is going to shift quite a bit, but in a way that's actually pretty exciting. Historically, a huge fraction of a mathematician's time goes into the grind: checking cases, verifying lemmas, chasing down whether some intermediate step actually holds, writing everything up rigorously. As AI systems get better at reasoning, and especially when you pair them with formal verification so you know the output is correct, a lot of that grind gets automated.

So what's left for humans? I think it's the parts that were always the most human anyway: deciding what's interesting. Mathematics isn't just a pile of true statements. It's a choice about which questions matter, which structures are beautiful, which connections between fields are worth pursuing. An AI can prove a million theorems, but someone has to say, "This is the direction that illuminates something," or "This conjecture, if true, would reshape how we think about this area."

I'd compare it to how mathematicians already relate to computers today. Nobody thinks a mathematician is diminished because they use a computer algebra system instead of doing the integrals by hand. The tools raised the level of abstraction people work at. I expect the same thing to happen, just much more dramatically. Mathematicians become more like architects or research directors. They set out a vision, sketch a strategy, and the system fills in and verifies the details at a scale no individual could manage.

And I think it'll open the field up, too. Right now, to contribute at the frontier you need years of training just to be able to verify your own work. If verification becomes something the machine handles, more people with good intuition and taste can participate. Over time you might see mathematicians tackling problems that were previously out of reach simply because the proofs were too long or complex for humans to hold in their heads. That's where I think the real payoff is. Not replacing mathematicians, but letting them ask much bigger questions.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that mathematicians will work with AI systems that automate verification and proof details, describing this as a more dramatic extension of current computer use.

r002.rationale: It does not raise the possibility that human input could worsen AI mathematical performance.

r003.rationale: It says mathematicians will choose interesting questions and pursue connections, but does not say they will redefine what mathematics encompasses.

r004.rationale: It says humans will choose which questions matter and ask bigger questions, even as AI proves theorems and fills in details.

r005.rationale: The response describes mathematicians setting a vision and strategy, but does not say they will decide which problems receive substantial AI reasoning resources.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's going to look a lot like what happened with chess, but with one big difference. In chess, once the engines got better than the humans, the humans basically became spectators and commentators. In math, that's not going to happen, because math is not a closed game. There's no fixed board. The hardest part of mathematics has always been deciding what's worth proving, what questions actually matter, what definitions carve the world at the right joints. That's a taste problem, not a search problem, and I don't think it goes away just because the search gets automated.

So the near-term picture is that the mathematician becomes something closer to a research director. You have a system that can grind through the technical lemmas, check your work formally, maybe propose ten candidate approaches to a problem overnight. And your job shifts to steering. Which of these directions is interesting? Which of these generalizations is actually the right one? Is this proof telling us something, or is it just true? A lot of great mathematicians already work this way with their students and collaborators. The AI just makes that leverage available to everyone, not just the people who run large groups.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that this makes mathematicians less important. I think it's the opposite. When proof becomes cheap, the bottleneck becomes judgment, and judgment is exactly what humans have spent centuries building up in this field. There's a reason we care about the Riemann hypothesis and not some arbitrary statement about integers. That reason lives in people.

Longer term, honestly, I think the discipline changes shape. You'll see mathematicians spending more time on exploration, on reading machine-generated proofs and extracting the ideas from them, on building the formal libraries that let the systems work at all. Some of that will feel less romantic than the lone genius at the chalkboard. But the actual experience of understanding something new for the first time, I don't think that gets taken away from anyone. It just gets to happen more often.

r001.rationale: The response describes a near-term role where mathematicians steer AI systems that generate approaches, check proofs, and handle technical lemmas.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that human input could eventually make AI mathematical performance worse.

r003.rationale: It says mathematicians shape definitions and that the discipline may change, but does not clearly say they can redefine what mathematics encompasses.

r004.rationale: It identifies deciding what is worth proving and which questions matter as human contributions that remain even when proof search is automated.

r005.rationale: It says mathematicians will steer AI toward interesting directions, but does not say they will allocate substantial AI reasoning resources among problems.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematicians will spend less time on the mechanics of proving a particular statement and more time deciding what’s worth proving. A lot of mathematical work involves exploring examples, trying approaches that don’t work, and filling in technical details. As AI gets better at those tasks, a human could explore many more ideas than they can today.

But choosing a good question is itself a deep mathematical skill. What would help us understand something? Which definition makes a complicated situation clearer? What connects two areas that seem unrelated? I expect that kind of judgment and taste to become more central.

And I wouldn’t assume those things are forever beyond AI, either. The role will keep changing. But in the nearer term, I think the exciting possibility is that a mathematician with these tools can take on problems that would otherwise be too expensive or too time-consuming to explore.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematicians using AI tools in the nearer term to explore more ideas and take on problems that would otherwise be too costly or time-consuming.

r002.rationale: It says AI may eventually develop judgment and taste, but does not raise the possibility that human input could worsen AI’s mathematical performance.

r003.rationale: It discusses choosing questions and definitions, but does not present mathematicians as redefining what mathematics encompasses.

r004.rationale: It identifies choosing good questions as a deep human skill that will remain central as AI takes on proving and technical work.

r005.rationale: It says mathematicians will decide what is worth proving, but does not say they will allocate substantial AI reasoning resources among problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematicians will spend less time on the mechanics of proving something and more time deciding what’s worth proving. A lot of mathematical work involves exploring an idea, getting stuck, trying a different approach, and checking details. As AI gets better, it can take on more of that exploration and verification, so a person can pursue ideas that would otherwise be too expensive to investigate.

But choosing good questions is a very deep part of mathematics. What’s an interesting definition? What connects two areas that seem unrelated? What would actually help us understand something? I think human judgment will remain important there, even as AI contributes more.

And I wouldn’t assume that division stays fixed forever. If systems become good at proposing interesting questions, too, the role changes again. My hope is that the overall effect is to make mathematicians more ambitious—to let them work on problems they wouldn’t have dared to tackle before.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematicians using AI for exploration and verification while pursuing more ambitious ideas, indicating a productive period of human–AI collaboration.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that human input could worsen AI’s mathematical performance.

r003.rationale: It mentions choosing interesting definitions and questions, but does not present mathematicians as redefining what mathematics encompasses.

r004.rationale: It says choosing good questions will remain a deep part of mathematics and human judgment will remain important as AI takes on more exploration and verification.

r005.rationale: It says mathematicians will decide what is worth proving, but does not say they will allocate substantial AI reasoning resources among problems.
